title: The mind is dyed
hookLine: your mind takes the color of the thoughts you keep (Meditations 5.16)
last: GIVING GRAPES IS WHAT VINES DO.

lines: THE THOUGHTS YOU KEEP IN THE WATER.
cards: Drop a white T-shirt into a pot of hot water with one red sock. It doesn't take much, and it doesn't take long. Everything comes out pink.
Now run through the thoughts that go round in your head on a normal day. The comment someone made at work. The worry about money.
The replay of an argument you already lost. Or the song you love, the kid's joke, the thing you're grateful for. You don't choose every thought that shows up.
But some of them you keep in the water, over and over. Marcus noticed what that does.

teach.h: THE SOUL IS DYED BY THE THOUGHTS.
teach.b: Here's the line from Book Five, in George Long's translation: "Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts."
Dyed is a strong word. Dye that takes doesn't sit on the surface. The color goes all the way through and won't wash out.
It isn't what you think once that shapes you. It's what you think habitually, the thoughts you dip into every day.
So Marcus tells himself to dye his soul on purpose, with a steady run of good thoughts, and gives an example.

teach.h: YOU CAN LIVE WELL IN A PALACE, TOO.
teach.b: Where a person can live, he says, they can also live well. Then he tests it on himself. Someone might say, but I have to live in a palace.
Fine, he answers: a person can live well in a palace, too. Remember who's writing. The palace was his actual address.
He isn't dreaming of a quiet cabin. He's telling himself that the life he's stuck with can still be lived well, because the color of it comes from inside.
Psychologists today have a name, rumination, for a thought on repeat. Marcus used the picture of a dye pot. You can't stop every thought from coming.
You can choose which ones you keep dipping into.

how: Many readers of the Stoics keep a few short lines to return to through the day, and some write them on cards or repeat them at set times, the way Marcus repeated his own reminders.

o: thinking slowly before a big decision
going over the same thought again and again
a calm and quiet kind of meditation

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: become the character of your mind

s: Marcus says a single thought shapes your mind
it's habitual thoughts, the ones you keep dipping into, that dye the soul.
Marcus says a person can live well even in a palace
he was testing the idea on his own life. the palace was his address.
Marcus tells himself to dye his soul on purpose
with a steady run of good thoughts, like: where a person can live, they can live well.

games.q: you're Marcus. you've told yourself a person can live well anywhere. a voice objects: but you have to live in a palace. what do you write back?
o: then I can't live well; the palace ruins everything.
a person can live well in a palace, too.
I'll leave the palace and live in a cabin.
games.why: he answers that a person can live well in a palace too. the color of a life comes from inside.

practice: Let a few of your usual thoughts go by, and notice which ones come back most.

Then choose one you'd like to soak in instead, something true and steadying: I can live well even here, or this day is enough, or a line from a text you love. Say it slowly inside, a few times, and let it sink in.

wordCard.voice: Rumination, the name for a thought on repeat, like Marcus's picture of a mind dyed by the thoughts it keeps returning to. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: 'is dyed', 'is dipped'. Marcus's verb for what thoughts do to the soul.

carryVoice: Your line: dyed by thoughts. The color goes all the way through. Day one hundred ninety-three.

sources.q: Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts.
